# Section A — Multiple Choice

### Question 1

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **How to kill a dopamine neuron**?

- **A.** Nigrostriatal tract facilitates voluntary movement. Research on the motor functions of DA:.
- **B.** Apomorphine: agonist that stimulates D1 and D2 receptors; causes behavioral activation. Amphetamine: drug that enhances dopamine release Relatively more dopamine on intact side.
- **C.** Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. DD mice exhibit severe aphagia (lack of feeding behavior), adipsia (lack of drinking), and hypoactivity; behaviors can be restored by L-DOPA.
- **D.** Mesolimbic dopamine pathway activates arousal and locomotor behavior; different neurons mediate the effects of rewarding and aversive stimuli. Mesocortical pathway: input to the PFC helps regulate cognitive functions such as attention and working memory.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
Nigrostriatal tract facilitates voluntary movement. Research on the motor functions of DA:.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The lecture uses loss of nigrostriatal dopamine function to investigate the contribution of that pathway to movement. Dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra project to the dorsal striatum; their degeneration in Parkinson's disease and experimental disruption in animal models support a role in motor function.

The key concerns the relationship between pathway integrity and behavior, not a practical method for producing neuronal injury. A lesion experiment asks how behavior changes when a defined system is disrupted, but interpretation must consider the location and specificity of the manipulation. Distinguish loss of dopamine synthesis or signaling from physical loss of the neuron itself; those interventions can produce related deficits without being biologically identical.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).
:::

### Question 2

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Neurobiology of ADHD – seminal PET studies Neurobiologyof ADHD–seminalPETstudies**?

- **A.** Deficits in sustained attention. Reduced grey matter volume in prefrontal cortex (structural MRI).
- **B.** Paradoxically low prefrontal catecholamine function. Noradrenaline.
- **C.** Reduced dopamine synthesis/activity in mPFCof ADHDpatients (Ernst et al. 1998). Radioactive DOPA.
- **D.** Methylphenidate: increases dopamine (DA) and noradrenaline (NA) levels in PFC and striatum (dorsal striatum and NAc) (Bymaster et al. 2002). NETinhibitor, atomoxetine:increases DAand NAonly in the PFC(Bymaster et al. 2002) Prefrontal cortex- NA DA.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
Reduced dopamine synthesis/activity in mPFCof ADHDpatients (Ernst et al. 1998). Radioactive DOPA.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The early PET examples use a dopamine precursor tracer to investigate aspects of dopamine synthesis or handling in specified regions. The lecture relates these findings to a hypothesis of reduced prefrontal dopaminergic functioning in ADHD. The interpretation depends on what the tracer signal represents and which comparison region is used.

This is different from directly counting receptors or measuring all dopamine activity with one universal scan. The lecture later introduces findings that complicate a single-deficit account, including receptor-availability comparisons and performance-related variation. The key should therefore be read as the reported interpretation of particular studies, not proof that every person with ADHD has the same measurable prefrontal dopamine abnormality.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

### Question 3

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Electrophysiological properties of serotonin neurons**?

- **A.** First demonstrated in cats: when awake, each nerve cell fires at a regular rate (tonic firing); become irregular with slow-wave sleep and stop firing during REM sleep. Research with DRN and MRN knockout mice: slow, tonic firing of DRN neurons promotes sleep (non-REM sleep); burst firing of the same cells favors a state of wakefulness.
- **B.** 14 receptor subtypes; 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A are most well known. 5-HT1A receptors: concentrated in the hippocampus, septal area, amygdala, and DRN; inhibit adenylyl cyclase to decrease cAMP synthesis; increase opening of K+ channels and membrane hyperpolarization 5-HT1A.
- **C.** 5-HT2A receptors occur in the cortex and other brain areas. Function via the phosphoinositide second- messenger system: increases Ca2+ levels in the postsynaptic cell; also activates protein kinase C (PKC).
- **D.** Ligand binds to a GPCR/receptor. The receptor activates PLC (phospholipase C).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
First demonstrated in cats: when awake, each nerve cell fires at a regular rate (tonic firing); become irregular with slow-wave sleep and stop firing during REM sleep. Research with DRN and MRN knockout mice: slow, tonic firing of DRN neurons promotes sleep (non-REM sleep); burst firing of the same cells favors a state of wakefulness.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The lecture presents observations from different preparations rather than one simple rule that “serotonin causes wakefulness.” Earlier cat recordings associated regular firing with waking, more irregular activity with slow-wave sleep, and cessation during REM sleep. The later mouse work described on the slide distinguishes slow tonic activity from bursts, with different consequences for sleep and waking.

The central lesson is that **firing pattern, cell population, and experimental method matter**. Observing activity during a behavioral state is not the same as manipulating that activity and demonstrating an effect on the state. Preserve those distinctions when comparing the findings; they should not be collapsed into a claim that every increase in serotonergic activity necessarily has the same effect on sleep.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).
:::

### Question 4

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Distribution of AChRs in the brain Let’s focus on the striatum**?

- **A.** Conditioned stimuli can have a motivational effect. You see a crackpipe on the ground (CS).
- **B.** The lecture treats **Pavlovian to instrumental transfer in the rat** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.
- **C.** Distribution of AChRs in the brain Let’s focus on the striatum.
- **D.** Local cholinergic interneurons (CINs) for form a microcircuit with dopamine neuron terminals in striatum. Dopamine terminals have β2 subunit containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
Distribution of AChRs in the brain Let’s focus on the striatum.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The figure shows **regional differences in nicotinic receptor subunit combinations**, including receptors in the caudate-putamen, basal forebrain, temporal cortex, and cerebellum. It then directs attention to the striatum, where the following slide examines local cholinergic regulation of dopamine terminals.

This connects anatomy to pharmacology: a receptor's location and composition help determine which circuit a drug can influence. Detecting receptors in a region does not mean every cell there synthesizes ACh. The original keyed option merely repeats the slide heading, so it does not actually identify a distribution or mechanism. Use the figure and subsequent striatal circuit to learn the concept, but treat this item as needing substantive answer choices before formal assessment.

### Question 5

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Measuring LTP in the laboratory Stim**?

- **A.** AMPAreceptors need tofirst depolarize theneuronenough to removetheMg2+block. NMDA receptors can then be activated and allow both Na+ and Ca2+intothecell Short-term potentiation – it happens first.
- **B.** CREB can lead toformationof retrograde messenger, nitricoxide (NO). NO travelsfrompostsynapticcell to presynaptic axon and triggersgreater release ofpresynaptic glutamate.
- **C.** CREB can lead toformationof retrograde messenger, nitricoxide (NO). NO travelsfrompostsynapticcell to presynapticaxon and triggersgreater release ofpresynapticglutamate.
- **D.** Measuring LTP in the laboratory Stim Record.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
Measuring LTP in the laboratory Stim Record.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The figure separates **stimulation of an input pathway from recording the postsynaptic response**. Its hippocampal example shows stimulation of Schaffer-collateral input and recording in the CA1 region. The accompanying traces illustrate a larger postsynaptic EPSP after LTP induction than before, following a comparable presynaptic event.

This comparison tests a change in communication between cells, not simply the existence of electrical activity. A bigger response is meaningful only relative to the baseline and the controlled test input. The original keyed phrase, “Stim Record,” labels the apparatus but does not explain the measurement. A substantive answer should identify where stimulation and recording occur and what before-versus-after change would count as evidence of potentiation.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

### Question 7

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Cool little spinning trick**?

- **A.** Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. DD mice exhibit severe aphagia (lack of feeding behavior), adipsia (lack of drinking), and hypoactivity; behaviors can be restored by L-DOPA.
- **B.** Mesolimbic dopamine pathway activates arousal and locomotor behavior; different neurons mediate the effects of rewarding and aversive stimuli. Mesocortical pathway: input to the PFC helps regulate cognitive functions such as attention and working memory.
- **C.** All are metabotropic receptors; D1 and D2 are most common. D1 receptors stimulate adenylyl cyclase – increasing the rate of cAMP synthesis.
- **D.** Apomorphine: agonist that stimulates D1 and D2 receptors; causes behavioral activation. Amphetamine: drug that enhances dopamine release Relatively more dopamine on intact side.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
Apomorphine: agonist that stimulates D1 and D2 receptors; causes behavioral activation. Amphetamine: drug that enhances dopamine release Relatively more dopamine on intact side.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A unilateral dopamine-system lesion creates an imbalance between the two sides. Amphetamine depends on available presynaptic dopamine mechanisms, so its effect is greater on the relatively intact side. Apomorphine acts directly at dopamine receptors and can reveal altered postsynaptic sensitivity on the denervated side.

The resulting rotation is therefore a behavioral readout of asymmetry, not proof that all dopamine-enhancing drugs act identically. The relevant contrast is **enhancing transmitter output** versus **direct receptor stimulation**. To interpret the experiment, identify which side retains functioning terminals and which receptors may have adapted after loss of input. The abbreviated key names the drugs, but the mechanistic explanation is what accounts for their differing effects.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).
:::

### Question 8

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Neurobiologyof ADHD–animalstudies**?

- **A.** DAT/NETblocker (antagonist) D-amphetamine (Adderall; Dexedrine). Inverse DAT/NETagonist - reverses the transporter X X ➔ ➔ ADHDpharmacology.
- **B.** Methylphenidate: increases dopamine (DA) and noradrenaline (NA) levels in PFC and striatum (dorsal striatum and NAc) (Bymaster et al. 2002). NETinhibitor, atomoxetine:increases DAand NAonly in the PFC(Bymaster et al. 2002) Prefrontal cortex- NA DA.
- **C.** Deficits in sustained attention. Reduced grey matter volume in prefrontal cortex (structural MRI).
- **D.** Paradoxically low prefrontal catecholamine function. Noradrenaline.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
Methylphenidate: increases dopamine (DA) and noradrenaline (NA) levels in PFC and striatum (dorsal striatum and NAc) (Bymaster et al. 2002). NETinhibitor, atomoxetine:increases DAand NAonly in the PFC(Bymaster et al. 2002) Prefrontal cortex- NA DA.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The animal-study comparison emphasizes regional selectivity. In the presented results, methylphenidate increases catecholamine measures in prefrontal and striatal regions, whereas atomoxetine's reported dopamine and norepinephrine increases are concentrated in prefrontal cortex. Their transporter actions therefore do not translate into an identical regional pattern.

A NET inhibitor can affect dopamine in prefrontal cortex because local clearance mechanisms differ from those in dopamine-rich striatal systems. The key concerns the specific study comparison, not an absolute statement about every dose, species, or brain region. Connect transporter target, regional anatomy, and measured extracellular transmitter before predicting behavior. Similar clinical aims do not mean that two drugs have the same pharmacological mechanism.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

### Question 9

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **There are LOTS of different serotonin receptors**?

- **A.** 5-HT2A receptors occur in the cortex and other brain areas. Function via the phosphoinositide second- messenger system: increases Ca2+ levels in the postsynaptic cell; also activates protein kinase C (PKC).
- **B.** Ligand binds to a GPCR/receptor. The receptor activates PLC (phospholipase C).
- **C.** DOI and related drugs are hallucinogenic in humans. Hallucinogenic effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) may stem from its ability to stimulate 5-HT2A receptors.
- **D.** 14 receptor subtypes; 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A are most well known. 5-HT1A receptors: concentrated in the hippocampus, septal area, amygdala, and DRN; inhibit adenylyl cyclase to decrease cAMP synthesis; increase opening of K+ channels and membrane hyperpolarization 5-HT1A.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
14 receptor subtypes; 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A are most well known. 5-HT1A receptors: concentrated in the hippocampus, septal area, amygdala, and DRN; inhibit adenylyl cyclase to decrease cAMP synthesis; increase opening of K+ channels and membrane hyperpolarization 5-HT1A.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Serotonin's effects depend on which receptor subtype it activates. The lecture's 5-HT1A example links receptor activation to **reduced adenylyl cyclase activity, less cAMP, and increased potassium-channel opening**. These changes can hyperpolarize the membrane and reduce the likelihood of firing.

Location adds another layer. A 5-HT1A receptor on a serotonergic neuron can function as an autoreceptor, reducing that neuron's activity; the same subtype on another neuron acts postsynaptically. Therefore, an inhibitory cellular effect does not translate automatically into one predictable behavioral effect throughout the brain. The listed brain regions help identify possible sites of action, but identifying the region and receptor location requires additional evidence beyond a systemic drug response.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).
:::

### Question 10

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Pavlovian to instrumental transfer**?

- **A.** Conditioned stimuli can have a motivational effect. You see a crackpipe on the ground (CS).
- **B.** The lecture treats **Pavlovian to instrumental transfer in the rat** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.
- **C.** Phasic DA response (FSCV).
- **D.** DhβE: selective blocker of of β2 subunit nAChRs. Optogenetic stimulation of striatal CINs blocks PIT.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
Conditioned stimuli can have a motivational effect. You see a crackpipe on the ground (CS).
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer occurs when a **reward-predicting cue changes the performance of an independently learned action**. Pavlovian learning establishes the cue–outcome relationship; instrumental learning establishes that an action produces an outcome. During transfer, presentation of the cue can invigorate the action.

The lecture's drug-cue example illustrates how an object associated with prior reward can acquire motivational significance. Merely recognizing the object is not the full phenomenon: the important result is a change in goal-directed effort or responding. Likewise, performing a previously rewarded action without a cue is instrumental behavior but not, by itself, evidence of transfer. The distinction lies in the interaction between the two forms of learning.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).
:::

### Question 11

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **AMPAand NMDA receptors ✤ AMPAand NMDA receptorsmediate**?

- **A.** CREB can lead toformationof retrograde messenger, nitricoxide (NO). NO travelsfrompostsynapticcell to presynapticaxon and triggersgreater release ofpresynapticglutamate.
- **B.** Excitotoxicity: excessive exposure to glutamate kills neurons. Cell death can occur by necrosis, characterized by lysis or by programmed cell death (apoptosis).
- **C.** AMPAreceptors need tofirst depolarize theneuronenough to removetheMg2+block. NMDA receptors can then be activated and allow both Na+ and Ca2+intothecell Short-term potentiation – it happens first.
- **D.** CREB can lead toformationof retrograde messenger, nitricoxide (NO). NO travelsfrompostsynapticcell to presynaptic axon and triggersgreater release ofpresynaptic glutamate.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
AMPAreceptors need tofirst depolarize theneuronenough to removetheMg2+block. NMDA receptors can then be activated and allow both Na+ and Ca2+intothecell Short-term potentiation – it happens first.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
AMPA-mediated excitation can depolarize a postsynaptic neuron sufficiently to **relieve the NMDA channel's magnesium block**. With glutamate and the required co-agonist present, the unblocked NMDA channel can then carry calcium as well as sodium. Calcium supplies the intracellular signal that links this brief electrical event to subsequent plasticity mechanisms.

Do not interpret the slide's shorthand as saying glutamate cannot bind an NMDA receptor at resting voltage. The assigned chapter distinguishes ligand binding from ion flow: magnesium can block the channel even when the required ligands are bound. Nor must AMPA be the only possible source of depolarization. It is the source emphasized in this example of cooperation between two glutamate receptor classes.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).
:::

### Question 13

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Ascending dopamine pathways have been implicated in several important behavioral functions**?

- **A.** All are metabotropic receptors; D1 and D2 are most common. D1 receptors stimulate adenylyl cyclase – increasing the rate of cAMP synthesis.
- **B.** D2 receptors have a higher affinity for DA than D1 receptors. Hypothesis: tonic DA release activates higher-affinity D2 receptors; increase in DA levels produced by phasic release additionally activates the lower-affinity D1 receptors.
- **C.** Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. DD mice exhibit severe aphagia (lack of feeding behavior), adipsia (lack of drinking), and hypoactivity; behaviors can be restored by L-DOPA.
- **D.** Mesolimbic dopamine pathway activates arousal and locomotor behavior; different neurons mediate the effects of rewarding and aversive stimuli. Mesocortical pathway: input to the PFC helps regulate cognitive functions such as attention and working memory.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. DD mice exhibit severe aphagia (lack of feeding behavior), adipsia (lack of drinking), and hypoactivity; behaviors can be restored by L-DOPA.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The dopamine-deficient mouse separates a transmitter's function from destruction of the whole neuron. The animals show severe reductions in feeding, drinking, and activity, and L-DOPA restores these behaviors by bypassing the missing synthesis step. This supports a role for dopamine in activating and organizing behavior, not simply in the physical ability to swallow or grasp food.

The existing key oversimplifies the genetic design. **Chapter 5 specifies that tyrosine hydroxylase is knocked out and then restored in DBH-expressing noradrenergic cells**, preserving norepinephrine synthesis. Merely leaving the DBH gene intact would not explain preserved synthesis upstream of its substrate. This source clarification is essential to understanding what the model selectively tests.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

### Question 14

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Neurobiologyof ADHD–PETstudies**?

- **A.** Deficits in sustained attention. Reduced grey matter volume in prefrontal cortex (structural MRI).
- **B.** Paradoxically low prefrontal catecholamine function. Noradrenaline.
- **C.** DAT/NETblocker (antagonist) D-amphetamine (Adderall; Dexedrine). Inverse DAT/NETagonist - reverses the transporter X X ➔ ➔ ADHDpharmacology.
- **D.** Classic stimulant side effects. Dizziness, insomnia, loss of appetite, anxiety, nausea, cardiovascular effects (ex. tachycardia).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
Deficits in sustained attention. Reduced grey matter volume in prefrontal cortex (structural MRI).
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The lecture combines structural and molecular imaging findings, which must be kept separate. Reduced gray-matter volume is a structural MRI result, whereas a PET radioligand can provide information about receptor availability. Equivalent receptor availability does not imply identical structure, transmitter release, or task performance.

The presented studies also relate striatal dopamine measures to attentional performance across diagnostic groups. This complicates the idea that every observed difference is unique to ADHD. The key identifies only part of the evidence. A careful interpretation specifies the modality and measured quantity for each result, then distinguishes a group comparison from a performance association and from the effect of methylphenidate.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

### Question 15

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Deeper look at the IP3 signaling pathway**?

- **A.** The lecture treats **There are heaps of serotonin receptors** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.
- **B.** Ligand binds to a GPCR/receptor. The receptor activates PLC (phospholipase C).
- **C.** DOI and related drugs are hallucinogenic in humans. Hallucinogenic effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) may stem from its ability to stimulate 5-HT2A receptors.
- **D.** Sodium in and potassium out. Fast neuronal excitation.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
Ligand binds to a GPCR/receptor. The receptor activates PLC (phospholipase C).
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The pathway begins with ligand binding to a G-protein-coupled receptor and proceeds to **phospholipase C (PLC)**. PLC cleaves PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ moves through the cytosol to receptors on the endoplasmic reticulum, where it triggers calcium release into the cytosol. DAG and calcium then support activation of protein kinase C.

Follow the sequence rather than memorizing disconnected abbreviations. The receptor detects the extracellular signal; the intracellular messengers distribute it; calcium and kinase activity help generate the cellular response. The calcium increase described here comes from an intracellular store, not necessarily from calcium entering through the receptor itself. That distinction separates this metabotropic pathway from direct opening of an ionotropic receptor channel.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).
:::

### Question 16

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Pavlovian to instrumental transfer in the rat**?

- **A.** Phasic DA response (FSCV).
- **B.** DhβE: selective blocker of of β2 subunit nAChRs. Optogenetic stimulation of striatal CINs blocks PIT.
- **C.** Acetylcholine (ACh; adjective form, cholinergic); synthesized in one step from choline and acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl CoA), catalyzed by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT). ChAT is found only in neurons that use ACh as a transmitter.
- **D.** The lecture treats **Pavlovian to instrumental transfer in the rat** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
The lecture treats **Pavlovian to instrumental transfer in the rat** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The slide's diagram separates three stages. First, a neutral cue is paired with reward. Second, an action such as lever pressing is trained to obtain reward. Finally, the cue is presented while the action is available, allowing comparison of **responding during the cue with responding without it**. Increased responding during the reward-predicting cue is the transfer effect illustrated.

Testing without normal reward delivery helps distinguish the cue's motivational influence from new reinforcement during the test. The keyed option in this MCQ is only a topic placeholder and does not describe these stages. The diagram provides the substantive answer; a valid assessment should ask about the separate learning histories, test comparison, or interpretation instead of rewarding recognition of the heading alone.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

### Question 17

### Question 18

Which statement correctly describes **Biosynthesis of GABA**, rather than the nearby topic **GABA transport**?

- **A.** GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid) major inhibitory amino acid transmitter; manufactured only by GABAergic neurons; has a critical role in regulating brain excitability. Synthesized from glutamate in one step by glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD).
- **B.** GABA is metabolized to glutamate and succinate by GABA aminotransferase (GABA-T), in neurons and astrocytes. In astrocytes, the glutamate is converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase.
- **C.** Co-release of GABA has been demonstrated for neurons that also use glycine, ACh, DA, or glutamate. In some cases there is co-expression of the vesicular transporters for multiple transmitters in the same neuron.
- **D.** Many brain areas are rich in GABA. Cortex and hippocampus: GABAergic neurons are interneurons.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid) major inhibitory amino acid transmitter; manufactured only by GABAergic neurons; has a critical role in regulating brain excitability. Synthesized from glutamate in one step by glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD).
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The integration point is that **GABA synthesis helps establish the inhibitory capacity of a circuit**. GAD converts glutamate to GABA, after which vesicular transport, release, and receptor activation are still needed for an inhibitory signal to occur. Making the transmitter is necessary to the cycle but is not the whole process.

This connects to the lecture's transporter and receptor examples. Reducing synthesis can decrease the available inhibitory transmitter, whereas inhibiting uptake can prolong its extracellular availability. Activating a GABA receptor directly is a third intervention, acting at the receiving cell rather than at transmitter production. Distinguishing these sites explains why drugs can alter GABAergic transmission through different mechanisms even when their broad effect is described as increasing or decreasing inhibition.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

This is why dopamine should not be reduced to a single “pleasure chemical.”

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}

The lecture links reduced GABA synthesis to increased susceptibility to excessive excitation and convulsions. This explains GABA's role in regulating network excitability, rather than merely labeling it “inhibitory.” Its synthesis-inhibitor examples are experimental pharmacology, not substances to use for self-experimentation. A correct explanation identifies the precursor, enzyme, product, and consequence of disrupting the pathway.

### Question 29

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Multiple ways to die**?

- **A.** Ischemic brain damage. One mechanism of ischemia.
- **B.** They don’t seem to work… JAMA. 2001;285(13):1719-1728. doi:10.1001/jama.285.13.1719 2001;286;(21):2673-2682. doi:10.1001/jama.286.21.2673.
- **C.** Necrosis happens slowly due to indirect effects of excitation (e.g., lysis). Osmotic swelling.
- **D.** Cerebrovascular disorder of sudden onset. Infarct.

**Correct answer: C.**

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The substantive distinction is between **lytic cell injury and programmed cell-death mechanisms**. Necrosis can involve osmotic swelling, membrane rupture, and release of cellular contents. Programmed death involves regulated biochemical processes; apoptosis includes removal of cellular material without the same pattern of lytic spillage.

The original keyed timing statement should not be treated as settled. Lecture slide 22 describes necrosis as slow and apoptosis as fast, whereas Chapter 8 describes relatively rapid necrosis under intense exposure and delayed programmed death. The chapter also distinguishes adult programmed necrosis from apoptosis and assigns different roles to synaptic GluN2A and extrasynaptic GluN2B receptors. These are explicit source discrepancies requiring instructor review; they cannot support a unique timing-based answer as currently written.

### Question 30

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **GABA transport**?

- **A.** Vesicular GABA transporters (VGAT) move GABA (and glycine) into vesicles. GABA is removed from the synaptic cleft by transporters GAT-1 and GAT-2 (in neurons and astrocytes) and GAT-3 (only in astrocytes).
- **B.** GABA is metabolized to glutamate and succinate by GABA aminotransferase (GABA-T), in neurons and astrocytes. In astrocytes, the glutamate is converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase.
- **C.** Co-release of GABA has been demonstrated for neurons that also use glycine, ACh, DA, or glutamate. In some cases there is co-expression of the vesicular transporters for multiple transmitters in the same neuron.
- **D.** Many brain areas are rich in GABA. Cortex and hippocampus: GABAergic neurons are interneurons.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
Vesicular GABA transporters (VGAT) move GABA (and glycine) into vesicles. GABA is removed from the synaptic cleft by transporters GAT-1 and GAT-2 (in neurons and astrocytes) and GAT-3 (only in astrocytes).
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
VGAT and GAT transporters act at **different membranes and stages**. VGAT loads GABA into intracellular synaptic vesicles, whereas GAT proteins remove released GABA from the extracellular space into neurons or astrocytes. Confusing these steps reverses the predicted effect of transporter inhibition.

The lecture's tiagabine example inhibits GAT-1, reducing uptake and increasing extracellular GABA availability. It does not directly fill vesicles or activate GABA receptors as an agonist. The subsequent receptor response still depends on the GABA present and the receptors available. This is the same reasoning used earlier to distinguish vesicular monoamine transporters from DAT or SERT: “transport blocker” is incomplete unless the transporter and direction of transport are specified.

Subtypes within those families differ in signaling, distribution, and function, so naming the transmitter alone does not specify the response.

The original answer is only a statement that the topic is important; it supplies no receptor distinction and is not an adequate substantive answer. For revision, be able to contrast 5-HT1A inhibition of cAMP signaling, 5-HT2A phosphoinositide signaling, and rapid 5-HT3 channel-mediated excitation. The current MCQ should be improved before formal grading rather than treating its placeholder as proof of mastery.

### Question 34

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Acetylcholine biosynthesis**?

- **A.** ACh is loaded into synaptic vesicles by vesicular ACh transporters (VAChT). VAChT can be blocked by vesamicol – reduces amount of ACh released when neurons fire.
- **B.** Botulinum toxins A through G are produced by the anaerobic bacterium Clostridium botulinum. The toxin proteins are taken up selectively by peripheral cholinergic nerve terminals, including at the neuromuscular junction and fibers innervating smooth muscle and secretory glands.
- **C.** Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) breaks ACh down to choline and acetic acid; four subunits combine to form a tetramer (G4). Three forms of AChE:.
- **D.** Acetylcholine (ACh; adjective form, cholinergic); synthesized in one step from choline and acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl CoA), catalyzed by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT). ChAT is found only in neurons that use ACh as a transmitter.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
Acetylcholine (ACh; adjective form, cholinergic); synthesized in one step from choline and acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl CoA), catalyzed by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT). ChAT is found only in neurons that use ACh as a transmitter.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Acetylcholine synthesis joins **choline and an acetyl group supplied by acetyl-CoA**, using choline acetyltransferase (ChAT). The product is acetylcholine, and neurons using it are described as cholinergic. ChAT therefore identifies a synthetic function, rather than a receptor or a transporter.

The lecture emphasizes precursor availability and neuronal activity as influences on synthesis. Distinguish ChAT from acetylcholinesterase (AChE): the former makes ACh, whereas the latter breaks released ACh down. Also distinguish synthesis from vesicular loading, which uses VAChT. Following these separate steps prevents the common mistake of assuming that any drug reducing cholinergic transmission must directly inhibit ChAT; the course's examples often act instead on uptake, storage, or release.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).
:::

### Question 35

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Stroke**?

- **A.** Glutamate occurs naturally in food and contributes to the umami flavor, which is essentially savoriness. Pure MSG is delicious, but glutamate is toxic, right?.
- **B.** Cerebrovascular disorder of sudden onset. Infarct.
- **C.** Ischemic brain damage. One mechanism of ischemia.
- **D.** They don’t seem to work… JAMA. 2001;285(13):1719-1728. doi:10.1001/jama.285.13.1719 2001;286;(21):2673-2682. doi:10.1001/jama.286.21.2673.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
Cerebrovascular disorder of sudden onset. Infarct.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A stroke is a **sudden cerebrovascular event**. The lecture distinguishes hemorrhage, involving bleeding, from ischemia, involving inadequate blood supply. It identifies an infarct as an area of dead or dying tissue and the surrounding penumbra as important to the discussion of further injury.

The point of introducing these terms is to connect a vascular problem to cellular consequences. Reduced blood supply can disrupt the energy-dependent processes that normally maintain ion gradients and regulate neurotransmitter availability. Subsequent excitotoxic signaling is one proposed contributor to damage, not the definition of stroke itself. The answer's two short labels therefore need the vascular distinction and tissue context; neither “infarct” nor “glutamate toxicity” alone describes every aspect of the event.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 23. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).
:::

### Question 36

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Astrocytes are important with GABA too**?

- **A.** Co-release of GABA has been demonstrated for neurons that also use glycine, ACh, DA, or glutamate. In some cases there is co-expression of the vesicular transporters for multiple transmitters in the same neuron.
- **B.** Many brain areas are rich in GABA. Cortex and hippocampus: GABAergic neurons are interneurons.
- **C.** Thalamus Thalamus.
- **D.** GABA is metabolized to glutamate and succinate by GABA aminotransferase (GABA-T), in neurons and astrocytes. In astrocytes, the glutamate is converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
GABA is metabolized to glutamate and succinate by GABA aminotransferase (GABA-T), in neurons and astrocytes. In astrocytes, the glutamate is converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Astrocytes contribute to **GABA metabolism and precursor recycling**, as they do for glutamate. Chapter 8 explains that GABA breakdown begins with GABA aminotransferase and proceeds through multiple steps toward succinate, with glutamate generated in the pathway. Astrocytic glutamate can then be converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase.

Glutamine can return to neurons, be converted back to glutamate, and supply GABA resynthesis through GAD. The original key compresses this into a single sentence; it should not be read as a complete one-step chemical equation. The important connection is that transmitter removal does not merely dispose of material: metabolic cooperation between neurons and glia also helps maintain the substrate needed for later signaling.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).
:::

### Question 38

Which statement correctly describes **Organization and function of the central noradrenergic system**, rather than the nearby topic **Adrenergic receptors THE AUTORECEPTOR**?

- **A.** NE neurons in the brain are located in the pons and medulla, especially in the locus coeruleus (LC). All neurons in the LC express the enzyme DBH and synthesize NE.
- **B.** Motor impulsivity (impulsive action). Impaired response inhibition/inhibitory control.
- **C.** Impulsivity scales and questionnaires. Barratt impulsiveness scale (BIS).
- **D.** Cognitive impulsivity. Delay discounting.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
NE neurons in the brain are located in the pons and medulla, especially in the locus coeruleus (LC). All neurons in the LC express the enzyme DBH and synthesize NE.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The central noradrenergic system is an anatomical projection system, whereas an adrenergic autoreceptor is one molecular feedback mechanism within it. The locus coeruleus and related brainstem groups provide norepinephrine-containing projections to many targets. DBH expression supports the transmitter identity of those neurons.

An autoreceptor detects the neuron's own released transmitter and can regulate further firing or release. The keyed option describes the origin and chemical identity of the system, not the complete receptor mechanism. The connection is that broad projection systems still require local regulation. A change in autoreceptor signaling can alter output from a neuron whose axons influence many distant regions.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).
:::

### Question 39

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Serotonin in anxiety**?

- **A.** 5-HT has a key role in regulation of anxiety. SSRIs and 5-HT1A receptor agonists are used to treat anxiety disorders.
- **B.** Are anxiety-regulating 5-HT1A receptors postsynaptic or presynaptic?. Experiments show that excitation of the serotonergic nerve terminals (increases 5-HT release) had an anxiolytic effect – increased time in open-arm of elevated plus-maze; inhibition of the terminals was anxiogenic.
- **C.** Serotonin influences hunger and eating behavior. Neurons in AN secrete α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH), and neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP).
- **D.** Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. A functional TH sequence is placed under DBH regulatory control A point of clarity.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
5-HT has a key role in regulation of anxiety. SSRIs and 5-HT1A receptor agonists are used to treat anxiety disorders.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The lecture brings together pharmacological and genetic evidence for serotonin's involvement in anxiety. It describes anxiolytic effects of 5-HT1A agonists in experimental animals and increased anxiety-like behavior in 5-HT1A-knockout mice. These observations support a role for the receptor, but do not by themselves identify the responsible brain region or receptor location.

That limitation is central to the answer. A systemically administered agonist can act at both autoreceptors and postsynaptic receptors, and a whole-animal knockout has broad consequences. It would therefore be premature to conclude that one particular serotonergic projection mediates the effect. The following lecture example narrows the question by manipulating nerve terminals and examining behavior in a defined circuit.

### Question 40

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Compounds affecting acetylcholine storage and release**?

- **A.** Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) breaks ACh down to choline and acetic acid; four subunits combine to form a tetramer (G4). Three forms of AChE:.
- **B.** Enzyme. Substrate.
- **C.** ACh is loaded into synaptic vesicles by vesicular ACh transporters (VAChT). VAChT can be blocked by vesamicol – reduces amount of ACh released when neurons fire.
- **D.** Botulinum toxins A through G are produced by the anaerobic bacterium Clostridium botulinum. The toxin proteins are taken up selectively by peripheral cholinergic nerve terminals, including at the neuromuscular junction and fibers innervating smooth muscle and secretory glands.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
ACh is loaded into synaptic vesicles by vesicular ACh transporters (VAChT). VAChT can be blocked by vesamicol – reduces amount of ACh released when neurons fire.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
VAChT packages acetylcholine into **synaptic vesicles**, making it available for regulated release when the terminal is activated. Vesamicol blocks this packaging step, so less transmitter can be released even if ACh synthesis and the arrival of an action potential still occur.

The lecture contrasts storage blockade with toxins affecting release itself. Botulinum toxin prevents vesicle fusion, while black widow spider venom is described as promoting massive peripheral ACh release. These are different interventions in the same signaling sequence. Identify whether the change concerns transmitter production, vesicle filling, or fusion with the terminal membrane. The keyed option concerns filling vesicles, not receptor antagonism or enzymatic breakdown of ACh after it reaches the synaptic cleft.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).
:::

### Question 41

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Glutamate toxicity in stroke**?

- **A.** Ischemic brain damage. One mechanism of ischemia.
- **B.** They don’t seem to work… JAMA. 2001;285(13):1719-1728. doi:10.1001/jama.285.13.1719 2001;286;(21):2673-2682. doi:10.1001/jama.286.21.2673.
- **C.** Glutamate occurs naturally in food and contributes to the umami flavor, which is essentially savoriness. Pure MSG is delicious, but glutamate is toxic, right?.
- **D.** Glutamate: ionized form of glutamic acid (an amino acid); formed from glutamine by glutaminase. Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
Ischemic brain damage. One mechanism of ischemia.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The lecture connects ischemia to **excessive extracellular glutamate and injury to nearby neurons**. Loss of adequate blood supply compromises normal cellular function, and disrupted glutamate regulation can lead to prolonged activation of excitatory receptors. The preceding receptor discussion explains why sustained ion entry, especially calcium signaling under pathological conditions, can become damaging.

This mechanism motivates efforts to protect tissue around an infarct. It does not mean glutamate is the initial vascular blockage or the only pathway of ischemic damage. The clinical-treatment question is separate: even if excitotoxicity contributes to injury, blocking one receptor class must still be shown to improve outcomes safely under actual treatment conditions. That is why the next slide discusses unsuccessful NMDA-blocker trials.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 24. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).
:::

### Question 42

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Co-release of GABA is common**?

- **A.** Thalamus Thalamus.
- **B.** The lecture treats **GABAergic interneurons** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.
- **C.** Co-release of GABA has been demonstrated for neurons that also use glycine, ACh, DA, or glutamate. In some cases there is co-expression of the vesicular transporters for multiple transmitters in the same neuron.
- **D.** Many brain areas are rich in GABA. Cortex and hippocampus: GABAergic neurons are interneurons.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
Co-release of GABA has been demonstrated for neurons that also use glycine, ACh, DA, or glutamate. In some cases there is co-expression of the vesicular transporters for multiple transmitters in the same neuron.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The co-release examples challenge a strict **one-neuron/one-transmitter rule**. The lecture describes GABA release from neurons also associated with glycine, ACh, dopamine, or glutamate. In some cases multiple vesicular transport systems coexist; in others, packaging involves transport machinery ordinarily associated with another transmitter.

Co-release does not make the two transmitters functionally identical. Simultaneous glutamate and GABA signaling can have different effects on the target cell because their receptors and conductances differ. This allows finer control than labeling a whole neuron simply “excitatory” or “inhibitory.” The evidence to look for concerns transmitter handling and release, not merely whether a molecule can be detected somewhere inside the cell for metabolic reasons.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).
:::

### Question 44

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Organization and function of the central noradrenergic system**?

- **A.** Impulsivity scales and questionnaires. Barratt impulsiveness scale (BIS).
- **B.** NE neurons in the brain are located in the pons and medulla, especially in the locus coeruleus (LC). All neurons in the LC express the enzyme DBH and synthesize NE.
- **C.** Adrenergic receptors THE AUTORECEPTOR.
- **D.** Motor impulsivity (impulsive action). Impaired response inhibition/inhibitory control.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
NE neurons in the brain are located in the pons and medulla, especially in the locus coeruleus (LC). All neurons in the LC express the enzyme DBH and synthesize NE.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Noradrenergic cell bodies are concentrated in brainstem groups, especially the locus coeruleus, but their projections reach many distant regions. The enzyme dopamine beta-hydroxylase is important because it converts dopamine toward norepinephrine synthesis and helps identify the noradrenergic phenotype.

The key concerns anatomical origin and transmitter identity. It does not imply that norepinephrine acts only in the locus coeruleus. Extensive projections allow this relatively localized system to influence arousal, sensory processing, and cognition across the forebrain and other targets. The lecture also connects it to familiar catecholamine mechanisms—vesicular storage, reuptake, metabolism, and tonic or phasic activity—so anatomy and transmitter handling should be understood together.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).
:::

### Question 45

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Identifying the precise anxiety-modulating mechanism**?

- **A.** Serotonin influences hunger and eating behavior. Neurons in AN secrete α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH), and neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP).
- **B.** Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. A functional TH sequence is placed under DBH regulatory control A point of clarity.
- **C.** Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT) neurotransmitter used by serotonergic neurons. Serotonin is an indoleamine.
- **D.** Are anxiety-regulating 5-HT1A receptors postsynaptic or presynaptic?. Experiments show that excitation of the serotonergic nerve terminals (increases 5-HT release) had an anxiolytic effect – increased time in open-arm of elevated plus-maze; inhibition of the terminals was anxiogenic.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
Are anxiety-regulating 5-HT1A receptors postsynaptic or presynaptic?. Experiments show that excitation of the serotonergic nerve terminals (increases 5-HT release) had an anxiolytic effect – increased time in open-arm of elevated plus-maze; inhibition of the terminals was anxiogenic.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The experiment narrows the anxiety question by manipulating **serotonergic nerve terminals**, rather than simply administering a drug throughout the body. In the lecture's account, terminal excitation increases serotonin release and increases open-arm time in the elevated plus-maze; terminal inhibition produces the opposite, anxiety-like pattern.

The lecture interprets this evidence as supporting a contribution from postsynaptic 5-HT1A receptors in the studied circuit. The logic is that increasing transmitter delivery to target cells reduces the measured anxiety-like behavior, rather than reducing transmitter output through autoreceptor inhibition. Keep the scope specific: open-arm time is a behavioral index, not a direct report of subjective anxiety, and the finding does not establish that every serotonergic projection has the same function.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 23. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).
:::
